one_liner: C2Rust-transpiled, fully unsafe Rust build of the ixy user-space 10G NIC driver; 91 vs 94 cycles per packet against C.
what_it_does: ixy is an educational user-space driver for Intel ixgbe NICs (82599ES/X520, X540, X550) that maps the device through sysfs or vfio-pci, sets up DMA rings in hugepages and receives and transmits packet batches without a kernel driver; the benchmark app forwards packets between two ports and increments one byte of each packet. This entry is not the idiomatic ixy.rs rewrite but a C2Rust transpilation of the C driver, mentioned in a five-line addendum to Rust-vs-C-performance.md (commit e543831, 'rust can be faster than C :)'). The transpiled code itself is not published in the ixy-languages organisation (13 repositories, none of them a C2Rust build), so there is nothing to integrate; the useful artefacts are the C driver (emmericp/ixy) and the safe Rust driver (ixy-languages/ixy.rs).
how_it_is_fast: C2Rust turns the C into unsafe Rust that keeps raw pointers and has almost no bounds checks, so the hot loops match the C logic; the document reports 121 instead of 127 instructions per packet and gives no further mechanism. One plausible, untested source of those 6 instructions: the C build compiles ixgbe.c, memory.c and ixy-fwd.c separately with no -flto, so pkt_buf_alloc (called per received packet) and pkt_buf_free (per sent packet) are out-of-line cross-file calls, whereas rustc optimises a whole crate and can inline across its modules. The safe ixy.rs driver is a different story: it executes about 65% more instructions (bounds checks, wrapper objects) that the out-of-order core mostly hides (IPC 2.09 vs 1.35).
when_to_use: Evidence when planning a C-to-Rust migration with C2Rust: the transpiled, unsafe stage of a packet-processing hot path need not be slower than the original C on the same LLVM.
Studying the cost of Rust safety in a driver: the same document quantifies bounds checks (6% more cycles at batch 32, 11% at batch 8) and integer overflow checks (0.8% throughput at batch 8).
Learning user-space NIC drivers on Linux x86-64 with an ixgbe-family card or virtio, using the published C driver or ixy.rs (about 1000 to 2000 lines each).
Reproducing per-packet counter methodology: perf stat with the ocperf wrapper on a forwarder under full bidirectional 64-byte load (issue #6).
when_not_to_use: As a library or driver to deploy: the C2Rust build is unpublished, and ixy.rs itself says it is not production-ready and that DMA may corrupt memory.
As proof that Rust codegen beats C: the gain is 3 cycles per packet (about 3%, derived) from one unreplicated run, with no variance, batch size, compiler versions or flags given.
Where you need safety: the faster variant is wholly unsafe transpiled code; the safe idiomatic driver is 6-11% slower in cycles per packet.
Non-Intel or non-x86 NICs and hosts: only ixgbe-family devices and virtio are supported, and the drivers need hugepages plus root or an IOMMU with vfio-pci.

integration.form: not published (transpiled driver); the related ixy.rs is a Cargo crate and ixy C is a CMake project
integration.dependencies: ixy.rs: libc, byteorder, log, lazy_static; ixy C: none beyond libc and Linux sysfs/vfio
integration.min_toolchain: not documented for the C2Rust build; ixy.rs uses edition 2018; the main counter table used gcc 6.3 for C and roughly Rust 1.36 nightly (issue #6)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 with an Intel 82599/X520, X540 or X550 NIC (ixgbe, ixgbevf in ixy.rs) or virtio; hugepages required
integration.thread_safety: not documented for the C2Rust build; the forwarder is single-threaded and the README recommends one process per RSS queue instead of shared threads

gotchas: Harness gaps: the C2Rust claim is two sentences added on 2019-10-30, after the ANCS 2019 paper (whose abstract, seen as a search snippet, reports only the safe driver: 63% more instructions, 4% slower); the transpiled source, rustc and clang versions, flags, batch size and number of runs are not given, and the clang comparison's own cycle count is not stated.

Baseline build: ixy C is compiled with -g -O2 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer and no -flto (unchanged since the 2017 initial import), while Rust optimises a whole crate at opt-level 3; the maintainer reports -O3 was sometimes slightly slower than -O2 (issue #6), so -O2 is not a crippled baseline, but the missing LTO is an untested confound for the 6-instruction difference.

The safe-Rust rows are not a pure bounds-check measurement: ixy.rs prefetches every received packet with _mm_prefetch (T1) in rx_batch (commit c734821, May 2019, gated on target_feature sse, which x86_64 targets have by default), while ixy C has no prefetch, which matches the table's C-only L2 and L3 hits (1.1 and 0.9 per packet at batch 32).
Hardware differs across the repo: the counter table ran on a Xeon E3-1230 v3, the README throughput graphs on an E3-1230 v2 at 3.3 and 1.6 GHz, and the latency plots on a Xeon E5-2620 v3.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Unlike libbzip2-rs or fast_rsync, which ship Rust code you can link and measure against a C library, this is a measurement without an artefact; use it only as a data point that transpiled unsafe Rust can match C in a hot I/O path, and take the published ixy.rs if you need a working safe driver.
verified_claims_summary: With perf stat counters on a Xeon E3-1230 v3 forwarding 64-byte packets between two ixgbe ports, C ixy (gcc 6.3, -O2 -march=native) used 94 cycles and 127 instructions per packet at batch 32 (108 and 139 at batch 8); the C2Rust transpilation used 91 cycles and 121 instructions (batch size not stated) and was reported faster than a clang build on the same LLVM as well. The idiomatic safe ixy.rs used 100 and 120 cycles (209 and 232 instructions) at batch 32 and 8.
status_note: Finished: the summary repo's last change is PR #13 'typo in C2Rust name' (2022-12-14) and every driver is marked Finished, though ixy.rs still took a register-write fix on 2026-10-09; the summary repo is BSD-2-Clause and ixy.rs MIT, but the C2Rust driver behind the claim was never published, so only the C and safe Rust drivers can be reused.
